text:
Recent work supports testing transition evidence against strong popularity and order controls. Spotify’s 2026 study finds that recency-weighted pairwise transition models outperform reproduced Transformers on several benchmarks, including three Amazon datasets; this supports transition baselines but does not establish that a particular residual adds information beyond popularity. [Study](https://research.atspotify.com/2026/10/do-sequential-recommendation-benchmarks-require-higher-order-sequence-modelling). RecSys 2025’s “Disentangling User and Item Sequence Patterns” compares random shuffling with shuffling constrained by item availability, showing that apparent sequential signal can reflect user behavior, item availability, or both. [Paper](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748042). Neither result directly validates the proposed residual on the four RecHarness categories.

A diagnostic design suggested by these findings: compare full scores, residual removed, popularity removed, residual only, and shuffled-transition residuals on identical prefixes and candidate sets. Keep coefficients and training-derived normalization scales frozen during inference ablations; report retrained ablations separately. Construct shuffled controls from training transitions, preserving directed in/out counts—or weighted strengths when counts determine scores—and repeat across shuffle seeds. Report paired validation HR@10 differences, target-rank changes, component score contributions, and top-10 entries/exits, stratified jointly by training item frequency and transition support, including zero support. These are proposed diagnostics, not an exact protocol located in the searched papers. Improvement over popularity and shuffled controls would support useful transition structure; aggregate gains alone cannot distinguish it from a popularity shortcut. Interpret component removal as model sensitivity, without inferring causal user intent or unobserved conformity traits.
